newsitem.title: USA: Dow soars to close above 6,900 for first time.
newsitem.headline: Dow soars to close above 6,900 for first time.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average soared more than 100 points Wednesday to close above the 6,900-point level for the first time as a rally in technology stocks spread to the broader market.
The steep gains brought the world's most closely-watched blue-chip index near the 7,000 milestone. The Standard & Poor's composite index set a new high, and the Nasdaq index rose more than 2 percent.
The Dow ended up 103.52 points, or 1.51 percent, at a record 6,961.63, breezing through the old high of 6,883.90 set on Jan. 21.
In the broader market, advancing issues swamped declines 1,757 to 758 on heavy volume of 563 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The sweeping rally, helped by a strong dollar and powerful mutual fund inflows, left few sectors behind. Technology, financial, energy, gold mining and transportation shares all surged.

Analysts said the sudden burst of investors' confidence was rooted in the technology sector, which got a critical boost when semiconductor equipment maker Applied Materials Inc. reported surprisingly strong quarterly profits late Tuesday. Applied Materials surged 7 to 52-1/8.
The earnings triggered a sharp technology rally that quickly spread to the broader market.
"The Applied Materials results definitely helped," said Bill Meehan, an analyst at Prudential Securities.

"If you step back and look, we spent a good deal of January ratcheting up interest rates and that didn't break the market," he said. "Then we got some technology disappointments and even in the face of those we're having a strong rebound."
The renewed appetite for stocks came amid fresh reports that investors were pouring more cash into U.S. stock mutual funds.

The Investment Company Institute, a trade group, said net cash flows into such funds nearly doubled in January to $24 billion from $12.22 billion in December, but still not as high as the record $28.9 billion in January 1996.

Also lending support was the dollar, which worked its way still higher, gaining ground against both the German mark and the Japanese yen. The dollar ended at 1.6871 marks, up from 1.6773 late Tuesday, and at 124.25 yen, up from 123.28.

Concern has been raised about the impact of a rising dollar on earnings for U.S. multi-national corporations, but analysts said the currency's rise had broader implications that far overshadowed those worries.
"The more important factor is that a strong dollar has induced foreign investors to buy U.S. securities," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane.
"The big picture is that the flood of foreign money is far more important than the earnings implications for most of the market," he said.

Gold prices jumped on New York's Commodity Exchange, helping gold mining shares to one of their strongest sessions in weeks. Newmont Mining Corp. rose 2-1/4 to 41-1/4 and Homestake Mining Co. rose 7/8 to 14-3/4.
Energy shares continued to rebound from their recent weakness. Exxon Corp. climbed 1-3/8 to 103, Texaco Inc. rose 1-3/8 to 104-3/4 and Chevron Corp. jumped 2-3/8 to 69-1/8.
The Nasdaq Composite index jumped 27.45 points to 1,358.96.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 13.18 to a record 802.77. The American Stock Exchange index rose 3.86 to 593.10.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 5.79 to 419.88, a new high. The average share was up 60 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a new high of 7,678.653 up 117.411 or 1.55 percent.
